input: Gravity settlers are widely used for separating solids from process streams, and in the case considered here a gravity settler is to be used to remove activated sludge from a process stream. The sizing of the unit has been carried out on the basis of a design overflow rate of 0.57 m h-1, and at the design throughput of 271 m3 h-1 this gives rise to a required plan area of 475 m2. The overflow rate can be thought of as the upward velocity of the stream through the settler, and it is this quantity that has to be kept low enough for the sludge solids to be able to settle against the flow and be retained in the unit rather than carried over with the clarified stream. It is important to note, however, that the overflow-rate basis adopted for this design is a vendor rule for this particular solid, rather than a value that has been established by testing on the stream in question. Indeed, no settling test on the actual slurry has been run, which means that the extent to which the behaviour of the real slurry, with its own particle characteristics and its own response to the conditions in the feed, matches the behaviour that the vendor rule assumes remains unconfirmed at this stage. The area that has been derived from the rule should therefore be regarded as carrying this uncertainty with it, since any departure of the actual settling behaviour from the assumed basis would feed directly through into the performance of the settler as installed.
target: A gravity settler removes activated sludge from a process stream. The design overflow rate is 0.57 m h-1 at a throughput of 271 m3 h-1, giving a plan area of 475 m2. The overflow rate is the throughput per unit plan area, and it works as an upward velocity: sludge that settles faster than the overflow rate is retained, and sludge that settles more slowly is carried out with the clarified stream. Plan area is the horizontal area over which the stream rises through the settler, measured at the surface where the clarified stream leaves it, and the sludge blanket forms where the settling solids meet the rising stream. The plan area is therefore not a free choice once the rate is fixed; area is the throughput divided by the rate the solid is trusted to settle at, and every error in the rate appears in the area at the same proportion. In this design the rate is a vendor rule for this solid. No settling test on the actual slurry has been run. The rule was therefore set on other slurries of the same solid, not on the stream the settler will treat, whose particle condition and feed state govern the settling it will actually show. The stated area is exactly as reliable as that rule: if the actual slurry settles more slowly than the rule assumes, the settler is undersized in the same proportion, and the shortfall appears as solids in the clarified stream rather than as any change in the stated figures. The design is complete on its own terms, since rate, throughput and area agree with each other; what is missing is not arithmetic but evidence, and the missing evidence is a settling test on the slurry itself, run at the condition of the feed the settler will receive.
